statement: Incline pressing (around 30-45 degrees) biases the clavicular/upper head of the pectoralis major and grows the upper chest more than flat pressing.
nuance: Support is real but thin and conditional. EMG: the upper-pec head shows peak activation at ~30 degrees (Rodriguez-Ridao 2020), BUT 0 vs 30 deg was NOT statistically significant for the upper pec (p=0.688), and above 45 deg the anterior deltoid takes over while pec output falls. Crucially, EMG is the wrong endpoint (effect-vs-practical). The only LONGITUDINAL growth trial (Chaves 2020) does back the claim: an incline-only group grew the 2nd-intercostal (clavicular) pec thickness significantly more than flat-only or combined groups. That elevates this above pure mechanism. However: (1) it is a single small untrained-male study reporting an implausibly large ~62% upper-pec increase that SBS/MASS flag as an outlier; (2) general strength gains were equivalent across groups; (3) acute muscle-swelling data (Albarello, reviewed by SBS) directly contradicted it, showing flat bench produced similar upper-pec and greater mid-pec swelling. So the directional claim (incline favors upper-pec growth) is plausibly true, but rests on one odd study and the practical magnitude versus simply doing more pressing volume is uncertain.
population: Trained and untrained young men (growth trial in untrained men; EMG in trained men)

statement: Flat (horizontal) bench pressing biases the sternal/mid portion of the pectoralis major.
nuance: This is the better-supported half of the incline/flat story. EMG: sternal and costal (mid/lower) pec activation peaks at 0 degrees and falls significantly as the bench inclines (Rodriguez-Ridao). The growth trial (Chaves 2020) showed the flat-only group had the largest change in sternal-region EMG amplitude, and acute swelling data (Albarello via SBS) showed flat bench produced significantly greater mid-chest thickness/CSA swelling than incline. So both proxy AND the available longitudinal/swelling data converge that flat pressing emphasizes the mid pec. Effect-vs-practical caveat: the unique mid-pec growth ADVANTAGE of flat over incline still rests on swelling + one trial, not a clean hypertrophy RCT, but the convergence across measures makes this a confident directional claim.
population: Trained and untrained young men

statement: Combining incline and flat pressing in the same program maximizes overall pectoralis growth/strength versus doing either alone.
nuance: This is the textbook 'do both angles to maximize the stimulus' recommendation, and it is the only claim here with a direct test that came out NEGATIVE. Chaves 2020 explicitly hypothesized the combination group would maximize adaptations and found it did not: isometric strength gains were equivalent across flat-only, incline-only, and combined groups, and the combined group actually grew the upper pec LESS than the incline-only group (and no better than flat for the mid pec). EMG-change differences also failed to favor the combination at 3 of 4 sites. So while combining angles is reasonable for balanced development and variety (the RP rationale), the specific 'maximizes growth' claim is contradicted by the lone longitudinal study. Caveat: single untrained-male, once-weekly, 8-week design; specificity (more total volume per movement) may explain why focused groups did as well or better.
population: Untrained young men, 8 weeks, 1x/week

statement: A wide pronated grip on the lat pulldown preferentially recruits/grows the latissimus dorsi compared with a closer grip.
nuance: Rests on EMG/mechanism, not growth. Sperandei et al. directly compared a wide pronated pulldown to a reverse (supinated) grip and found the wide grip produced only a SMALL, statistically NON-significant increase in lat activation; the authors concluded grip-driven differences are small and 'may have no weight training significance.' An older EMG study (Signorile) did find a wide pronated front pulldown gave the highest lat EMG, so the activation literature is mixed, and even where it favors wide grip it is EMG only. No longitudinal study shows wide grip grows the lats more. Per the effect-vs-practical rule, an inconsistent activation edge is not proof of more growth. Honest read: grip width is a minor variable; pick what loads comfortably through a full ROM.
population: Trained men (EMG, isometric and 10-12RM dynamic)

statement: A supinated (underhand) pulldown grip shifts work to the biceps while a pronated grip preferentially trains the lats/back.
nuance: This common trainer/clinician claim is specifically tested and not supported. Sperandei found biceps brachii activation was statistically the SAME across all pulldown and row variations - supination did NOT preferentially activate the biceps. Lat activation was also not significantly different between pronated and supinated pulldowns. The only significant grip effect was a change in the lat:biceps RATIO (driven by tiny, individually non-significant shifts), which the authors judged too small to matter for training. So the folk rule that 'underhand = arms, overhand = back' is contradicted by the direct EMG evidence, and there is no growth evidence supporting it either.
population: Trained men (EMG)

statement: Horizontal rows bias the mid-back (rhomboids/mid-trapezius) while vertical pulldowns bias the lats.
nuance: The mid-back half is reasonably supported; the 'pulldowns are more lat' half is weaker. Sperandei found the seated row recruited the middle-trapezius/rhomboid group to a significantly GREATER extent than either pulldown - and it did so without sacrificing lat activation (row lat activity was equal-to-higher than pulldown). That gives a genuine activation basis for using rows to target the scapular retractors/mid-back. Caveat 1 (effect-vs-practical): this is EMG, not a regional-growth trial, so it is directional guidance, not proof of differential hypertrophy. Caveat 2: actively cueing scapular retraction during the row did NOT further increase mid-trap/rhomboid activity. Both movement classes train the lats; rows simply add more mid-back. The chest-supported-vs-bent-over distinction is mostly about removing lower-back/torso-stabilizer fatigue and cheating, not a proven lat-vs-mid-back shift.
population: Trained men (EMG)

statement: Rows are a poor lat exercise because the lat loses leverage and tension at the top, and lat-focused work should emphasize long muscle lengths (e.g., straight-arm pull-overs / lat prayers).
nuance: This is a coherent biomechanics/length-tension argument (Henselmans) but it is mechanism, not measured growth. The premises are anatomically sound: the lat has near-zero internal moment arm in full shoulder flexion (arms overhead) and in hyperextension (elbows behind torso), so a fully-retracted row loses lat leverage at the top and rows do not load the lat at long lengths. From this, lat prayers / straight-arm pulldowns are argued to keep tension across the lat's length with peak load near anatomical position. The effect-vs-practical rule applies hard here: there is NO head-to-head hypertrophy trial showing pull-overs or lat prayers grow lats more than pulldowns or rows. It is a plausible, well-reasoned selection heuristic - consistent with the genuine lengthened-position growth signal - but the specific exercise-superiority claim is unproven.
population: Mechanistic/EMG + moment-arm data; no human growth comparison

statement: Cable lateral raises are superior to dumbbell lateral raises because the cable keeps tension on the side delt in the stretched/lengthened (bottom) position where dumbbells offer almost none.
nuance: Pure resistance-curve mechanism with no direct growth test. The premise is true: with dumbbells the resistance moment arm is near zero at the bottom (arm hanging) and peaks near horizontal, so the lengthened position is essentially unloaded; a cable set up to pull across the body maintains tension low. Combined with the genuine (if modest) lengthened-position growth advantage seen elsewhere, this makes cables a reasonable choice to load the side delt at length. BUT (effect-vs-practical) there is no study comparing cable vs dumbbell lateral-raise HYPERTROPHY; even the lengthened-bias literature is for ROM/partials, not this specific exercise pair, and lateral-raise ROM at the shoulder is short. RP treats them as interchangeable rotation options and does not claim cable superiority. So this is a defensible mechanistic preference, not an evidence-backed 'more growth' claim.
population: Mechanistic; extrapolated from lengthened-training literature

statement: Behind-the-neck overhead pressing is superior (e.g., for the delts) to front/military pressing.
nuance: No growth advantage is demonstrated, and the variation carries a worse risk profile. Behind-the-neck pressing forces maximal external rotation + horizontal abduction, increasing subacromial/impingement and anterior-capsule stress, especially in lifters with limited shoulder mobility. Any claimed delt-targeting benefit is activation/mechanism-level at best; there is no hypertrophy or strength trial showing it beats a front press, which loads the same prime movers (anterior + lateral deltoid) through a safer path. Honest finding: front and behind-neck pressing are at best equivalent for the delts, so the added joint risk is not justified by an evidenced growth payoff. Note: the bench-press literature here is tangential but reinforces that as press paths get less favorable for the target, the anterior deltoid simply takes over more load without a clear hypertrophy gain.
population: General lifters; no direct growth comparison

statement: Dips and decline pressing preferentially train/grow the lower (sternocostal/costal) pectoralis major.
nuance: Activation-level support, no growth proof. Decline pressing reliably shows the highest lower/costal-pec EMG (Glass & Armstrong; Rodriguez-Ridao shows costal-pec activation peaks at 0 degrees and is greater than at inclined angles), and chest dips share a similar declined arm-path that biases the lower fibers. So a lower-pec activation bias is well established. But this is exactly the effect-vs-practical trap: there is no longitudinal study showing dips or decline press grow the lower pec MORE than flat bench, and the only regional-pec growth trial (Chaves) studied flat vs incline, not decline/dips. The flat bench already strongly loads the sternocostal pec. Reasonable directional heuristic, unproven hypertrophy superiority.
population: Trained men (EMG); no growth trial for decline/dips

statement: Lengthened-biased curls that load the stretched position (e.g., incline dumbbell curls) build the biceps more than shortened-position curls like preacher curls.
nuance: This is the one mechanism-flavored claim with real growth backing - but with two key corrections. (1) Training at LONGER muscle lengths does generally produce modestly MORE hypertrophy than training at shorter lengths: a meta-analytic subgroup found ~6.8% more growth for lengthened vs full-ROM training, and multiple RCTs (including direct biceps work comparing stretched-position vs peak-contraction curls) favor the lengthened position. So preferring the incline curl (long head loaded at a stretched shoulder position) over the preacher (peak loaded in the shortened position) is evidence-consistent. (2) Corrections per the recorded truth: this is NOT 'stretch-mediated hypertrophy' in the strict sense - the extra growth comes from training through long muscle lengths, not from a true stretch stimulus, and the magnitude is MODEST, not transformative. EMG-based versions of this argument are unreliable predictors. Best practice (RP) is to ROTATE both - incline for the stretch, preacher/spider for the shortened/peak position - rather than treat one as strictly superior. Verdict 'supported' because growth data, not just mechanism, back the lengthened-position direction.
population: Mostly untrained/recreational; some trained data; effect may shrink with training age

statement: Acute EMG activation (or acute muscle swelling/pump) reliably predicts which exercise will cause more regional hypertrophy.
nuance: This is the cross-cutting meta-claim that underwrites almost every activation-based exercise-selection argument above, and it does not hold. Surface EMG amplitude does not equal motor-unit recruitment or hypertrophic potential (Vigotsky), and the most direct test (SBS/MASS review of Albarello plus the Plotkin squat-vs-hipthrust analysis) found acute proxies fail to track longitudinal growth: in the pec study, EMG, muscle swelling, and the one existing incline/flat GROWTH trial pointed in three different directions (EMG: angle-specific; swelling: flat best everywhere; growth: incline best for upper pec). Correlations between acute proxies and real hypertrophy are weak (r roughly -0.03 to 0.5). Practical rule this establishes: an activation or swelling/pump difference is NOT evidence of more growth - demote any selection claim that rests on it to 'disputed' unless a hypertrophy or strength outcome backs it.
population: Trained lifters; applies across muscle groups

statement: Squatting to a deep range of motion (at or below parallel, full knee flexion) builds more quadriceps and overall leg muscle than partial/shallow squats.
nuance: This is one of the few depth claims with longitudinal growth/strength data behind it, not just activation. SBS's squat guide states plainly that 'deep squats help you gain more strength and muscle than shallow squats,' and the gmax systematic review notes that, while acute EMG for squat depth is contradictory (Caterisano found deeper = more GMax EMG but didn't equate load; Da Silva found partial squats produced HIGHER GMax EMG when load was equated), 'chronic studies have suggested that deeper squats, or a combination of ranges of motion, induce the most substantial functional and muscular gains' (Bloomquist 2013, Kubo 2019, Bazyler 2014). The mechanism is longer muscle length and greater time under tension at the bottom, where quad knee-extension demand peaks. Effect-vs-practical: the EMG picture is muddy and even reverses depending on load-equating, so the claim rests on the actual training studies showing more growth from full ROM, which is why it earns 'supported' rather than resting on activation. Caveat: most depth-vs-depth training studies are in untrained/recreational lifters, and 'deep' in studies is rarely true end-ROM.
population: untrained-to-recreationally-trained adults; mechanistically generalizes to trained but fewer direct trained-lifter trials

statement: A knee-dominant squat style (sitting straight down, more knee flexion ROM) builds quads better than a hip-dominant 'sit-back' style that shifts load to the hips.
nuance: SBS's squat guide makes the practical-experience case directly: sitting back reaches full hip flexion sooner and 'won't go through as much knee flexion, so your squat likely won't be optimal for quad growth,' and notes that lifters with great deadlifts but 'chicken legs' improve dramatically when they sit down into the squat and train quads through a longer knee-flexion ROM. The biomechanics support it: total knee+hip extensor demand at a given femur angle is fixed regardless of style, but a more knee-dominant pattern keeps the quads loaded through more knee-flexion ROM (longer quad muscle length). Effect-vs-practical: this is partly mechanistic/coaching wisdom plus the well-supported longer-ROM-grows-more principle rather than a head-to-head sit-back-vs-sit-down hypertrophy trial, so it is graded slightly lower than the depth claim. The headline is a within-quad emphasis tool, not a claim that one style grows more total leg muscle.
population: trained lifters (coaching/biomechanical inference); supported by longer-ROM growth principle

statement: Squat stance width changes the muscle bias: a wide stance shifts emphasis to the glutes/adductors, while a narrow stance emphasizes the quads.
nuance: This rests almost entirely on acute EMG and biomechanics, not growth. The gmax review cites Paoli (2009) finding larger stance widths (1.5-2x trochanter distance) yield greater GMax EMG, and a wider stance increases hip flexion/adductor involvement. But SBS's squat guide emphasizes that total summed knee+hip extensor demand at any given depth is identical 'regardless of bar position, stance width, or footwear' — stance changes how demand is distributed across positions, not the total, and SBS treats stance choice mainly as a comfort/depth/leverage decision. Effect-vs-practical: there is no longitudinal hypertrophy study in this corpus showing wide-vs-narrow stance produces meaningfully different quad-vs-glute growth, and EMG is a poor predictor of regional growth (per the regional-hypertrophy and stretch docs). The adductor-magnus contribution to hip extension at depth is real and large, so a wider/deeper stance plausibly trains adductors more, but 'glute vs quad' growth reallocation is unproven. Verdict disputed because it leans on activation/mechanism with mixed practical evidence.
population: trained lifters; EMG studies in resistance-trained men and women

statement: Foot position on the leg press (high/wide = more glute/hamstring; low/narrow = more quad) lets you bias which muscles the exercise trains.
nuance: This is a near-universal gym claim that rests on mechanics and presumed activation, with no direct longitudinal hypertrophy data in this corpus comparing foot positions on the leg press. The mechanistic logic is sound — a higher foot placement increases hip flexion ROM and hip-extensor (glute/ham) demand while reducing knee ROM, and a lower placement does the reverse, increasing knee-flexion ROM and quad demand — and RP's quad guide endorses varying foot stances across mesocycles to hit 'the many other muscles in your legs that quad training targets, such as the adductors.' Effect-vs-practical: per the squat-guide principle, summed knee+hip extensor demand at a given joint configuration is fixed; foot position redistributes ROM and leverage rather than adding net stimulus, and EMG/mechanism is not proof of differential GROWTH. A low foot position genuinely lengthens the quad's knee-flexion ROM (which the well-supported longer-length principle says should help quads), so the quad-biasing direction is more defensible than the glute/ham-biasing one. Disputed overall because the muscle-reallocation claim is mechanism-only.
population: general trainees; mechanistic/EMG inference

statement: Hip-hinge movements (RDL, stiff-leg deadlift, good morning) emphasize the hip-extensor hamstrings (biceps femoris long head, semimembranosus) plus glutes, while leg curls emphasize the knee-flexor hamstrings (semitendinosus, distal/short-head biceps femoris) — so both movement patterns are needed for complete hamstring development.
nuance: This is the strongest hamstring regional-bias claim, backed by both consistent EMG region-mapping AND a direct growth study. The hamstring-glute regional EMG paper shows hip-hinge/hip-extension exercises (RDL, step-up, hip extension) drive GMax and proximal/long-head BF + semimembranosus, while knee-flexion exercises (Nordic, leg curl) preferentially recruit semitendinosus and distal/medial BF; the leg curl elicited the LOWEST GMax of all six exercises. The growth-level confirmation comes via Maeo: seated (hip-flexed, hip-extensors lengthened) leg curl grew the hip-extensor hamstring heads more, and lengthened hip-hinge training (Maeo multi-hip) grew GMax, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, and BF long head ~2x more than shortened. Effect-vs-practical: the head-specific EMG would be 'activation only,' but because the recruitment split tracks each head's actual joint function (hip vs knee) AND the leg-curl-vs-hinge growth pattern matches it, this rises to 'supported.' RP's hamstring guide operationalizes it: program both a hip hinge and a leg curl essentially every week.
population: trained men and women; growth study (Maeo) in untrained/recreationally trained

statement: Increasing the stretch/ROM of a hip hinge — e.g., a deficit or step Romanian deadlift, or pulling to a deeper stretch — increases posterior-chain stimulus and hamstring/glute growth versus a shorter-ROM version.
nuance: Two tiers of evidence. The EMG RDL-variants study (Coratella) shows the step-RD (greater barbell displacement and trunk flexion, more posterior-chain elongation) significantly increased excitation of GMax, semitendinosus, and erector spinae longissimus vs both standard RD and stiff-leg DL — but EMG alone is not proof of growth. The growth-level backing comes from Maeo's lengthened-partial hip-extension study (cited in the stretch-hypertrophy doc), where training the hip extensors through the lengthened 90-45° range produced ~2x the hamstring/glute hypertrophy of full ROM, and from the broader longer-muscle-length literature. Effect-vs-practical: 'supported' because the longer-length / lengthened-bias direction is corroborated by hypertrophy trials, not just the EMG. Caveat the recorded truth carefully: more excitation in the step-RD is an activation finding; the GROWTH endorsement comes from the separate lengthened-training studies, and erector-spinae fatigue can limit how much extra hinge ROM is usable before the lower back gives out (RP caps hip hinges near 5-10 reps for this reason).
population: competitive bodybuilders (EMG); untrained/recreational (growth studies)

statement: The barbell hip thrust grows the glutes more than the squat because it produces far greater gluteus maximus EMG/peak-contraction loading.
nuance: This is the textbook case of activation NOT equaling growth. Contreras (2015) showed the hip thrust elicits roughly double the mean and peak upper/lower GMax EMG of the back squat at 10RM loads — but that paper's own conclusion calls for longitudinal studies before claiming superior hypertrophy. When the growth study came (Plotkin et al. 2023, cited in the stretch-hypertrophy doc), squats and hip thrusts produced broadly SIMILAR glute hypertrophy, and the much larger hip-thrust EMG did not translate into more glute growth — EMG was at best a weak, inconsistent predictor of regional glute growth (between-subjects r = -0.03 to 0.5). Mechanistically the squat trains the glutes at a longer muscle length (deep hip flexion) while the hip thrust loads them hardest at a short, shortened/peak-contracted length, and the longer-length principle favors the squat for growth. Verdict disputed because the popular claim rests on EMG/peak-contraction mechanism that the direct hypertrophy data contradicts; the honest finding is roughly equivalent glute growth (with the squat arguably edging it), so both belong in a program rather than the hip thrust replacing the squat.
population: trained women (EMG); trained/recreational adults (Plotkin growth study)

statement: The hip thrust biases the glutes toward their shortened/peak-contracted length while the squat (and deep hip hinges) load the glutes at a long/stretched length, so the two are complementary rather than redundant for complete glute development.
nuance: The length-position contrast is anatomically real and useful: in a hip thrust peak GMax tension occurs at full hip extension (glute shortened), whereas a deep squat or RDL loads the glute most at deep hip flexion (glute lengthened). RP's glute guide is built on programming both 'hip thrust movements' (maximal hip extension under load, peak-contraction holds) and 'compound hip-dominant movements' (deadlifts/squats with 'complete hip hinge with full glute stretch at bottom'). Effect-vs-practical: the complementary-length rationale is a sound mechanism, and the broader length literature suggests the stretched-position work (squat/hinge) may carry an independent growth advantage; however, there is no head-to-head trial proving you grow MORE glute by combining short- and long-length work than by doing more of either alone. So 'supported' as a complementary-coverage principle, but stop short of claiming a quantified additive growth benefit. Note this is the constructive flip-side of the disputed 'hip thrust grows glutes more' claim: the value of the hip thrust is the short-length/peak-contraction emphasis it adds, not superior total glute growth.
population: trained lifters; mechanistic + practitioner consensus

statement: The seated leg curl grows the hamstrings more than the lying/prone leg curl because the flexed-hip seated position trains the hip-extensor hamstring heads at a longer muscle length.
nuance: Backed by a direct MRI hypertrophy study, not activation. Maeo et al. (2021), as summarized in the SBS leg-extension article, compared seated (hip-flexed) vs lying/prone (hip-extended) leg curl training: because three of the four hamstring muscles are hip extensors, they are more lengthened in the seated position, and the seated curl produced greater hypertrophy of those hip-extensor hamstring heads. (Symmetrically, the sartorius — a hip flexor — is more lengthened in the lying curl and grew more there, confirming the 'every muscle trained at a longer length grew more' pattern.) Effect-vs-practical: this earns 'supported' because the evidence is longitudinal muscle growth from a within-participant design, the gold standard for this kind of comparison, rather than EMG. Practical caveats: the absolute difference, while real, is one of several reasons RP recommends including both seated and lying/standing curl variants across a week; and the finding is in a within-person model that prioritized size over strength.
population: untrained/recreationally trained adults (within-person MRI design)

statement: Standing (knee-extended) calf raises grow the gastrocnemius far more than seated (knee-flexed) calf raises, while the soleus grows about equally either way — so standing biases the gastroc and seated is mainly needed to target the soleus.
nuance: Backed by a direct MRI growth study, Kinoshita et al. (2023), a within-person 12-week trial. The biarticular gastrocnemius is lengthened with the knee extended (standing) and slack with the knee flexed (seated). Standing calf raise produced much greater gastrocnemius hypertrophy (lateral gastroc +12.4% vs +1.7%; medial +9.2% vs +0.6%; whole triceps surae +5.6% vs +2.1%; Cohen's d 0.88-1.58, large), and notably the gastroc showed essentially NO significant growth in the seated condition. The monoarticular soleus, unaffected by knee angle, grew similarly in both (2.1% vs 2.9%, trivial). Effect-vs-practical: this is unusually clean — actual muscle-volume growth, not EMG — so 'supported,' and it doubles as a textbook longer-muscle-length result. The standard practical takeaway holds: use standing/knee-extended raises to build the gastroc and seated/bent-knee raises specifically to reach the soleus; the often-repeated 'seated raise hits soleus' part is true, but 'seated also builds the gastroc' is effectively false.
population: untrained adults (within-person MRI design)

statement: Doing leg extensions with the hips more extended (reclined, ~40° vs 90° hip flexion) substantially increases rectus femoris growth without compromising vastus lateralis growth.
nuance: Backed by a direct within-participant growth study, Larsen et al. (2024), summarized in the SBS leg-extension article. The three vasti are monoarticular (knee only), so hip angle shouldn't affect them — and indeed vastus lateralis hypertrophy was equal at 40° vs 90° hip flexion. But the biarticular rectus femoris is a hip flexor as well as knee extensor, so a more extended hip (40°) lengthens it; that condition produced ~50-170% MORE rectus femoris growth, with the advantage largest proximally. This aligns with Mitsuya's MRI-activation work and the longer-length pattern. Effect-vs-practical: 'supported' because it is a true hypertrophy outcome. Two honest caveats the recorded truth demands: (1) interestingly, the rectus-femoris benefit appeared LARGER proximally than distally, somewhat at odds with the usual lengthened-training pattern, and the mechanism is unclear; (2) SBS's author still suspects exercises that lengthen the rectus femoris even more (reverse Nordic curl, sissy squat) may beat the leg extension for that muscle, since the leg extension omits 40-50° of bottom-end knee-flexion stretch. So the tweak is a confirmed within-exercise improvement, not necessarily the best rectus-femoris exercise overall.
population: untrained adults (within-participant design)

statement: Across lower-body muscles, training (or biasing partials) toward the lengthened/stretched position generally produces somewhat more growth than shorter-length training, and you should pick exercises that load the target muscle at long lengths.
nuance: The longer-muscle-length advantage is the connective thread under most of the other lower-body claims (deep squats, seated leg curl, standing calf raise, extended-hip leg extension, lengthened hip hinges), and the SBS stretch-hypertrophy review concludes lengthened training generally yields more hypertrophy (meta sub-group ~+6.8% vs full ROM; individual studies up to ~2x in calves and hip extensors), via greater fascicle-length (longitudinal) and modest pennation-angle gains. Critical nuance the recorded truth insists on: (1) it is almost certainly NOT 'stretch-mediated hypertrophy' — the few seconds per set at longer length are far too little stretch stimulus to cause the stretch-mediated effect seen in animal/long-duration human stretching; the mechanism is unresolved. (2) You do NOT need to train at end-ROM or feel a deep stretch to benefit — most studies showing the effect didn't train through maximal stretch. (3) EMG/activation differences and pump/swelling do NOT reliably predict which exercise grows a muscle more (Plotkin, Vigotsky), so the lengthened-position rationale should be applied via ROM/leverage, not EMG. (4) Magnitude is modest and partly studied in untrained lifters, with possible attenuation as training advances. Effect-vs-practical: 'supported' as a real growth-relevant heuristic, explicitly distinguished from the over-claimed 'stretch-mediated' framing.
population: mostly untrained/recreational; some trained data; broad meta-analytic base
